passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies a contested position within contract law, functioning as an equitable corrective to the rigid requirements of classical contract formation. Under orthodox contract doctrine, a binding agreement requires offer, acceptance, and consideration — the last being the exchange of something of legal value that distinguishes an enforceable promise from a mere gift. Yet courts have long recognized that this requirement, applied without qualification, can produce injustice when one party relies to its detriment on a promise that lacks formal consideration. Promissory estoppel addresses precisely this gap: it allows a court to enforce a promise, despite the absence of consideration, where the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee to rely on the promise, and where that reliance was both actual and detrimental.

The doctrine has, however, been applied with notable inconsistency across common-law jurisdictions. Consider two representative scenarios. In a 1971 decision by a New South Wales appellate court, a property developer promised a subcontractor that a longstanding discount on materials would continue for the duration of a major project. No formal contract was executed. When the developer later revoked the discount and demanded the full contract price, the court held that promissory estoppel operated as a complete defense, effectively extinguishing the developer's right to the higher price. But in a 1989 Ontario case involving an employer's informal promise to maintain a pension benefit, the court declined to apply promissory estoppel as a sword — that is, as an independent cause of action — and limited it to a defensive role, preventing the employer from denying the promise but awarding no affirmative relief to the employee. The divergence in outcomes illustrates that courts have not agreed upon whether promissory estoppel can generate new rights or merely prevent the unconscionable retraction of existing ones.

This asymmetry traces to a deeper doctrinal tension. Anglo-Australian courts, influenced by the broader equitable tradition, have tended to treat reliance-based estoppel as a substantive right, capable of founding an independent cause of action. North American courts, by contrast, have more frequently confined it to a defensive posture, treating it as a shield against bad faith rather than a sword of affirmative relief. The difficulty is that neither approach is fully coherent. A purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed whenever they have acted on a promise not in response to a threatened lawsuit but simply in anticipation of a benefit — the more common commercial situation. Yet an unconstrained offensive doctrine risks collapsing consideration doctrine altogether, since nearly any promissory statement made in a commercial context might generate reliance. The most defensible resolution, though one courts have been reluctant to embrace uniformly, would calibrate the availability of offensive promissory estoppel to the degree of reasonable reliance and the magnitude of the promisee's detrimental act, rather than categorically barring its use as a sword.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel was developed by Anglo-Australian courts as a substantive right and has since been adopted, in modified form, by North American jurisdictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inconsistent application of promissory estoppel across common-law jurisdictions reflects a deeper unresolved tension over whether the doctrine generates affirmative rights or merely prevents unconscionable retractions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts should abandon the consideration requirement in contract law and replace it with a unified standard based on detrimental reliance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 1971 New South Wales decision and the 1989 Ontario case demonstrate that promissory estoppel is routinely misapplied by lower courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine that fills the gap left by the consideration requirement and should be applied only as a defensive shield.

explanations.correct: The passage traces an inconsistency between the Anglo-Australian and North American treatments of promissory estoppel, locates the cause in a fundamental doctrinal dispute about whether the doctrine creates rights or only blocks retractions, and concludes with the author's proposed resolution. B captures this full arc.
explanations.A: Too narrow and historically inaccurate relative to the passage — the passage does not describe North America as adopting a modified Anglo-Australian view; it describes divergence, not adoption.
explanations.C: Too strong and not the author's claim; the author proposes calibrated offensive use, not wholesale abandonment of consideration.
explanations.D: The two cases are illustrations, not evidence of routine misapplication; this is the too-narrow trap fixating on the illustrative examples.
explanations.E: This restates the North American position, which the author actually critiques as incomplete — making it a paragraph-level restatement that omits the author's evaluative conclusion.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is introduced and defined; two cases illustrating conflicting applications are presented; the conflict is traced to a deeper tension and a preferred resolution is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal problem is identified; a historical account of how courts resolved the problem is provided; the author concludes that the resolution was satisfactory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing doctrines are compared; their historical origins are traced; and the author recommends that courts adopt the older of the two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine is defined; a single illustrative case is analyzed in depth; and the author argues that the case was wrongly decided.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An equitable principle is introduced; its abandonment by modern courts is documented; and the author proposes that it be revived through legislation.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces and defines promissory estoppel. Paragraph 2 presents two cases (New South Wales 1971 and Ontario 1989) with conflicting outcomes. Paragraph 3 traces the conflict to a deeper doctrinal tension and offers the author's preferred calibrated resolution. A maps this three-step structure exactly.
explanations.B: The author does not conclude that the resolution has been satisfactory — the author finds neither approach fully coherent, which is the opposite of a satisfied conclusion.
explanations.C: The passage does not compare two competing doctrines against each other; it analyzes one doctrine (promissory estoppel) with two different applications, and does not recommend the older approach.
explanations.D: There are two cases, not one, and the author does not argue that either was simply wrongly decided — the author diagnoses a systemic tension, not a single error.
explanations.E: The doctrine is not described as abandoned, and no legislative remedy is proposed — this introduces a move the passage never makes.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the 1989 Ontario case differed from the 1971 New South Wales case in that the Ontario court

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejected the principle of promissory estoppel entirely and refused to grant any relief to the promisee.

choices.label: B
choices.text: limited promissory estoppel to a defensive role and declined to award affirmative relief to the employee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: found that the employer's promise had been unsupported by any form of consideration and therefore unenforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: held that promissory estoppel could be used offensively but only where the detrimental reliance was substantial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: required the employee to demonstrate that reliance on the promise had been formally documented before granting any relief.

explanations.correct: The passage states that the Ontario court 'declined to apply promissory estoppel as a sword' and 'limited it to a defensive role, preventing the employer from denying the promise but awarding no affirmative relief to the employee.' B is a close paraphrase of this.
explanations.A: The Ontario court did not reject promissory estoppel entirely — it recognized the doctrine but confined it to a defensive posture. This is an altered-scope trap.
explanations.C: The passage does not say the Ontario court found the promise unenforceable for lack of consideration — the court used estoppel defensively, which is a different holding.
explanations.D: The passage says the opposite — the Ontario court rejected offensive use entirely; it did not calibrate offensive use to the degree of reliance.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention any formal documentation requirement imposed by the Ontario court; this introduces a detail from paragraph 2's discussion of aboriginal rights documentation (from the genre context), not from this passage.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The consideration requirement should be entirely eliminated from common-law contract doctrine in all jurisdictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court that categorically refuses to allow promissory estoppel as an offensive claim fails to protect promisees who acted in anticipation of a benefit rather than in defense against a lawsuit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Anglo-Australian approach to promissory estoppel is superior to the North American approach in every material respect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because consideration doctrine is foundational to contract law, any doctrine that threatens it should be rejected regardless of its equitable appeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts should treat oral promises in commercial settings as fully equivalent to written contracts for purposes of enforcement.

explanations.correct: The author states that 'a purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed whenever they have acted on a promise not in response to a threatened lawsuit but simply in anticipation of a benefit — the more common commercial situation.' B restates this inferential claim accurately.
explanations.A: The author proposes calibrating offensive estoppel, not abolishing consideration — this overreaches the author's stated position.
explanations.C: The author criticizes both approaches — noting that neither is 'fully coherent' — so endorsing Anglo-Australian superiority in every respect overstates the author's view.
explanations.D: This is essentially the position the author rejects — the purely defensive doctrine is what the author finds inadequate, so the author would not endorse this claim.
explanations.E: The passage does not address the oral vs. written distinction as a basis for enforcement; this is outside the scope of the author's argument.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the purely defensive application of promissory estoppel can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: strong approval, because it prevents the collapse of the consideration requirement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured endorsement, tempered by concern that it may occasionally disadvantage commercially sophisticated promisees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: critical acknowledgment of its partial validity, combined with the view that it is insufficient to address the most common commercial situations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: outright rejection, on the grounds that it represents a fundamental misreading of equity doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cautious neutrality, since the author refrains from assessing either the defensive or offensive approaches on the merits.

explanations.correct: The author acknowledges the concern behind the defensive approach — that an unconstrained offensive doctrine risks collapsing consideration — but then states that the defensive doctrine 'leaves promisees exposed' in 'the more common commercial situation.' This is a critical but not dismissive stance that recognizes partial validity while finding it insufficient. C captures both the acknowledgment and the criticism.
explanations.A: The author does not approve of the purely defensive doctrine; the author finds it inadequate, which is the opposite of strong approval.
explanations.B: The word 'endorsement' is too positive — the author explicitly criticizes the defensive-only approach as leaving promisees exposed, which is more than a tempered concern.
explanations.D: 'Outright rejection' overstates the author's tone; the author acknowledges the logic behind the defensive approach before criticizing it, and the criticism is grounded in practical inadequacy, not a charge of fundamental misreading.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral — the final paragraph contains explicit evaluative language ('A purely defensive doctrine leaves promisees exposed'; 'neither approach is fully coherent'; 'the most defensible resolution'), making neutrality clearly wrong.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 1971 New South Wales case and the 1989 Ontario case serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that the doctrine of promissory estoppel originated in Anglo-Australian courts and was later imported into North American jurisprudence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide concrete illustrations of the cross-jurisdictional inconsistency in the application of promissory estoppel introduced in paragraph one.

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that courts in both jurisdictions have reached erroneous results by misapplying the equitable principles underlying promissory estoppel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that the 1971 case was correctly decided whereas the 1989 case reflects an unduly restrictive interpretation of equitable doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that differences in outcomes between the two cases can be entirely explained by the different facts presented to each court.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 opens by stating that the doctrine has been applied 'with notable inconsistency across common-law jurisdictions' and then uses the two cases as illustrations of that inconsistency. B accurately identifies this illustrative function in relation to the paragraph's opening claim.
explanations.A: The passage does not argue for a direction of influence or importation; this is accurate content about the cases' jurisdictions but wrong about their function in the argument.
explanations.C: The author does not characterize either court as simply erroneous — the author presents them as reflecting different doctrinal approaches, then critiques both approaches in paragraph 3. 'Erroneous results' imposes a judgment the author does not make about the individual decisions.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the New South Wales result over the Ontario result; the author treats both as instantiating imperfect approaches and reserves judgment until paragraph 3.
explanations.E: The author attributes the divergence to doctrinal orientation, not to factual differences between the cases — in fact, the cases both involve informal promises upon which the promisee relied, suggesting the facts are structurally similar.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the resolution the author advocates for applying promissory estoppel offensively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court grants affirmative relief to a tenant who, relying on a landlord's assurance that a lease would be renewed, spent substantial funds renovating the property, even though no formal lease renewal was executed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court refuses to enforce an oral promise in a commercial transaction on the grounds that the promisee could have protected itself by insisting on a written contract.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court applies promissory estoppel as a complete bar to any claim by the promisor, regardless of the degree to which the promisee relied on the promise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court holds that consideration doctrine is so fundamental that promissory estoppel may never be used, whether defensively or offensively, to overcome its requirements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court allows a promisee to sue on an informal promise solely because the promise was made in writing, without inquiring into whether the promisee actually changed its position in reliance on the promise.

explanations.correct: The author advocates calibrating offensive promissory estoppel to 'the degree of reasonable reliance and the magnitude of the promisee's detrimental act.' Situation A presents precisely this: the promisee (tenant) acted in reasonable anticipation of a benefit (lease renewal), incurred substantial detrimental reliance (renovation costs), and a court grants affirmative relief accordingly. This matches the author's proposed calibrated offensive use.
explanations.B: This reflects a court declining to apply promissory estoppel altogether — the opposite of the author's recommended approach for cases of substantial detrimental reliance.
explanations.C: This describes an unconstrained offensive doctrine that the author explicitly warns would 'risk collapsing consideration doctrine altogether' — it is the very excess the author seeks to avoid.
explanations.D: This reflects the position that promissory estoppel should never be applied, which the author clearly rejects given the author's endorsement of a calibrated offensive use.
explanations.E: The author's resolution is grounded in the degree of actual reliance, not in the form of the promise — enforcing based on the written form alone without inquiring into reliance inverts the author's reasoning.
